title: The Republic, Plato
subtitle: 4th century BC AD
subject: litterature
description: To define justice, Plato imagines an ideal city and the myth of the cave. The Republic is not an electoral program: it is an investigation into the soul and power.

hero.hook: What if justice was better understood by drawing an entire city?

blocks.text: Around **380 BC**, **Plato**, Greek philosopher and founder of the Academy in Athens, wrote the **Republic**. In Greek, we say *Politeia*. The dialogue starts with a simple question: what is **justice**? To answer this, **Socrates**, central character in Plato's dialogues, proposes an astonishing detour: constructing in words an ideal city, the , the “beautiful city”. [[Kallipolis]]

This is not a fantasy novel. It's a **analogy**: understanding the city to understand the soul, and the soul to judge power. , a British philosopher and mathematician, would later say that all Western philosophy is just a series of footnotes to Plato. This book explains why. [[Alfred North Whitehead]]

sections.title: The soul and the city, same plan

blocks.text: Plato divides the soul into three parts. Desire, the , is linked to material appetites. Courage, the , is the seat of noble anger and strength of character. Reason, the , is capable of accessing the truth. The ideal city has three classes: producers, **guardians** soldiers, leaders. Justice is that each party does its job without encroaching on the others. [[Epithumia]] [[Thumos]] [[Logos]]

blocks.caption: Plato's Academy in Athens: thinking about the city to educate the soul.

blocks.text: The idea is still shocking: it links private morality and political organization. For Plato, an unjust city produces twisted souls. And a disordered soul produces a corrupt city. Justice is not just a decree. It is an inner and collective balance.

The ideal leaders are the , those who love truth more than power. They live without excessive private property. They have been trained for a long time in mathematics and **dialectic**, the art of dialogue which seeks the truth. Plato distrusts Athenian democracy, which condemned Socrates to drinking hemlock in 399. [[The philosopher-kings]]

, a 20th century philosopher, will accuse the Republic of announcing totalitarianism. Others see it as an educational utopia, not a police manual. The debate has remained open for twenty-five centuries. [[Karl Popper]]

Behind the political scheme, there is . The sensible world, the one we see and touch, is only a shadow. Governing well means seeing the **Good**, the Supreme Idea, not just managing fleeting opinions. [[Plato's Theory of Ideas]]

sections.title: The cave: emerging from the illusion

blocks.text: The **cave myth** is the most famous passage in the book. Chained prisoners see only shadows on a wall, cast by a fire behind them. One is released, goes out into the sun, returns to warn the others. They call him crazy. Education, says Plato, is not filling a vase. It is turning our gaze towards the light.

blocks.caption: Plato: to think is to agree to leave the familiar shadows.

blocks.text: This image has spanned the centuries: media, ideologies, intellectual comfort. Getting out of the cave costs. Staying in is reassuring. Plato suggests that the philosopher must return to enlighten others, even if he is mocked. Knowledge is not a private luxury. It's a responsibility.

sections.title: Regimes that rot, a work that remains

blocks.text: Plato also describes the decline of regimes: aristocracy, timocracy, oligarchy, democracy, tyranny. Each regime is born from the vices of the previous one. The lesson is not fatalism. It is vigilance: institutions follow the character of citizens.
The **Republic** links personal justice and political justice. Through the ideal city and the cave, Plato asks: what is the value of a power that does not seek truth?
